title: Rangers condemn ‘vile, cowardly’ graffiti referencing Ibrox disaster after Scottish Cup match vs. Celtic
content:
Rangers condemned “vile” and “cowardly” graffiti the club said had been found at the their stadium after Sunday’s Scottish Cup quarter-final against Celtic which referenced the Ibrox disaster.

Both clubs issued statements on Thursday in response to fan disorder during the Old Firm, which Celtic won on penalties after a 0-0 draw at Ibrox.

Rangers stated they would support a “fully independent review” into a number of incidents which occurred on Sunday, before adding they were “appalled to discover graffiti within the stadium” referencing the 1971 disaster at their home ground, where 66 people were killed in a crush on a stairway.

“What we can say now is that issues of stadium safety and the legacy of the Ibrox Disaster are deeply personal to this club,” Rangers’ statement read. “The memory of the 66 supporters who lost their lives in January 1971 deserves dignity and respect. To desecrate their memory is vile. It is cowardly. It is shameful. This is not football rivalry and it is not banter. It is the abuse of a tragedy that claimed 66 lives.”

Celtic also issued a statement on Thursday addressing the events from Sunday’s game. “There are clearly serious issues to be addressed and examples of unacceptable behaviour which require appropriate responses,” the statement read.

After Tomas Cvancara scored the winning penalty in the shoot-out, supporters from both sides entered the pitch with objects, with pyrotechnics appearing to be thrown in both directions. Police Scotland said after the match it would investigate the incident, which saw “a number” of arrests, and officers and members of the public injured. The Scottish Football Association (FA) described the scenes as “shameful”.

Speaking to Celtic’s in-house media, interim chairman Brian Wilson said it was “unfortunate” that events after the match “to some extent detracted or overshadowed” the result. Wilson added he was “disappointed” by the comments made by Police Scotland Chief Constable Jo Farrell, who expressed disappointment when speaking in Scottish Parliament on Wednesday that “nobody came out to condemn that violence“.

“Measuring responses by condemnatory statements isn’t really very accurate, if this could be resolved by statements of condemnation, it would have been resolved decades ago,” Wilson said. “It’s actions that matter and the way that we as a club handle these experiences and the way others handle these experiences. So I think if you’re going to ask for condemnation, you have to be more specific and there are certainly things which I would happily condemn and regret.”

He added that fans spilling onto the pitch has happened “numerous occasions this season alone” in Scotland and it “does not normally draw expressions of of condemnation”.

Wilson continued by saying evidence should be reviewed “before we create maybe a false narrative” and that if there evidence of a threat of violence, “then of course I’ll condemn that”.

Sunday’s game saw Celtic fans allocated the full Broomloan Road Stand at Ibrox for the first time since 2018, following years of reduced allocations for away supporters by both clubs, triggered by Rangers first doing so in December of that year.

Celtic’s statement said “concerns about access arrangements” for their supporters at Ibrox has been raised prior to the match. Both Rangers, and Celtic interim chairman Wilson, said they welcome the access and ticketing issues as part of the inquiry.

Rangers said the independent review “must be thorough and wide-ranging” and that “all parties must be prepared to have their actions and decision-making subjected to proper scrutiny”.
